extracted.intended_audience: instructors, meeting leaders and facilitators in academic training settings (e.g., graduate student instructors, trainer-leaders)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for preparing, conducting, and evaluating small-to-medium academic training meetings (roles: participant, leader, facilitator, recorder), handling difficult behaviors, and improving meeting design and instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting participant — Preparing for the meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: A meeting participant reviews the agenda before the meeting, confirms attendance or contacts the leader well ahead of the meeting to make alternative arrangements, and does whatever preparation is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assumes participants will read the outline; leaders may need direct action for particularly difficult individuals who do not prepare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting participant — Conducting the meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: A meeting participant knows the objectives ahead of time, arrives on time, keeps an open mind, helps ensure participation from everyone, sticks to agenda items during discussion or group work, suggests alternatives when appropriate, shares helpful ideas, supports and follows ground rules, and avoids creating difficult situations (and discourages others from doing so).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are behavioral expectations used to judge appropriate participation and to reduce disruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitator role — General
rubrics_metrics.description: The facilitator is concerned with the process of conducting the meeting: acts as time-keeper and referee, keeps the meeting running according to the plan, deals with problem people, and remains neutral to resolve disputes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not have the meeting leader mediate conflicts when the leader is a party to the dispute; neutral mediators are preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitator — Preparing for the meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: The facilitator develops objectives, reviews the agenda before the meeting, works with the leader on logistical problems, reads the plan to estimate timing for each part, does required preparation, and tries to identify and plan for difficult situations that may arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advance planning includes time allocations and contingency plans for anticipated problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitator — Conducting the meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: The facilitator focuses participants on relevant issues, stimulates discussion when appropriate, tries to get everyone to participate, monitors time spent on each agenda item, keeps the meeting running according to plan, protects people and their ideas from attacks, deals with difficult people/situations, remains neutral in conflicts, keeps discussions focused, and keeps small groups working productively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitator actions are both preventive (setting tone, timekeeping) and reactive (managing attacks, re-focusing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recorder — Preparing for the meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: The meeting recorder reviews the agenda before the meeting, confirms attendance or contacts the leader ahead of time to make alternative arrangements, and does any required preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recorder role may be optional for many training meetings; include when detailed records are useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recorder — Conducting the meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: The meeting recorder captures ideas without editing or paraphrasing, checks that information has been recorded correctly, and helps keep track of what has been accomplished in the meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recording is descriptive (accurate capture) rather than interpretive; recorder verifies and maintains a record of decisions and progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Side conversations — problem and solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: participants hold side conversations that disrupt the meeting. Solutions include stopping the meeting and asking the participant if they have an idea to share with the whole group, walking around and positioning near talkers, asking the participant a question about a recent point or the current discussion, or calling on the talker(s) by name and reminding them side conversations are distracting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many classroom management techniques transfer to meetings (direct engagement, proximity, calling by name).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominating participants — problem and solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: a participant monopolizes discussion or attempts to direct the meeting. Solutions include thanking the speaker and using the agenda/time constraints to refocus, using subtle body language/time signals (watch glance, shuffling papers) with caution, asking other participants for their thoughts, and acknowledging the speaker but offering to continue the conversation after the meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time-signals can backfire; prefer agenda-based redirection and soliciting others' input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disagreeable participants — problem and solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: participants who quibble, attack, or are combative. Solutions include paraphrasing their comments without loaded language, responding to the content rather than the attack, finding merit in a comment and moving on, and reminding the group of limited time with the option of continuing the discussion later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain calm, focus on content, and de-escalate by neutral paraphrase and moving to productive points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shy, quiet, or distracted participants — problem and solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: participants who do not participate sufficiently. Solutions include calling on reticent participants by name and asking for perspectives, having participants discuss with a neighbor before speaking to the whole group, taking the participant aside during a break to ask about reticence, and asking non-contributing group members to summarize the group's findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use small-group or pair strategies to build confidence before whole-group participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antagonistic participants — problem and solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: participants skeptical about the meeting's value or relevance. Solutions include circulating agendas before the meeting, starting with a statement of meeting objectives, ensuring the meeting is necessary before calling it, meeting one-on-one afterward if antagonism is personal, finding value in a participant's comments and paraphrasing them, and asking a time-consuming critic to continue the discussion after the meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-meeting communication and framing can prevent much antagonism; personal follow-up is often necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima donnas — problem and solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: participants who expect exceptional treatment or privileges. Solutions include (short-term) conceding requests cautiously, ensuring the prima donna has read responsibilities for meeting participants and asking how special requests serve that role, involving them in group discussion, and assigning them a concrete job (e.g., recorder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid setting long-term precedents by routinely caving; channel their energy into constructive responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confrontations in meetings — handling approach
rubrics_metrics.description: When a confrontation occurs, acknowledge the conflict, promise to resolve it after the meeting, and move on; follow up after the meeting to sort out the situation in a private setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In-meeting de-escalation preserves time and audience; private follow-up allows fuller resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of difficult meeting behavior — diagnostic insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficult situations often stem from an individualistic focus: participants ask 'what am I going to get out of this?' rather than 'what do I have to contribute?' This reduces sense of responsibility and participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigate via clearly assigning roles and communicating responsibilities; emphasize group-oriented expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gathering feedback — principles
rubrics_metrics.description: To make meetings more effective, gather information from participants as soon after the meeting as possible; ask for specific feedback with examples; encourage honest responses; and importantly, the meeting organizers must take feedback seriously and act on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delayed or ignored feedback can create negative feelings; immediate and specific feedback enhances improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model for improvement (Haynes-adapted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvement steps: you must want to change; gather information on the current situation; identify specific areas requiring improvement; find different ways to achieve objectives; actually do things differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A schematic/stepwise approach from desire to action guides systematic meeting refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting evaluation method — participant questionnaires
rubrics_metrics.description: Distribute questionnaires at the meeting end or ask participants to return them later. Immediate collection yields higher return; mailed/returned surveys often have low and biased return rates (50% is high).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of nonresponse bias: dissatisfied participants may be less likely to return questionnaires, skewing results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting evaluation method — observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Invite class observers to attend training meetings (conducted like an observational visit) or conduct a feedback visit; observers can be more objective than participants or leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feedback visits can yield rich information but require attention to meeting time constraints and potential observer effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting evaluation method — self-evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Meeting leaders should do a self-evaluation after each meeting, at minimum answering: (a) What went well? (b) What didn't go well? (c) What am I going to do about it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-evaluation is the minimum and can be done with facilitator input; it's useful for iterative improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus groups — structure and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus groups are short meetings with a leader and 3–5 participants, typically about six minutes per participant. Each participant prepares a 2–4 minute summary of what went well in their class and what they weren't satisfied with; other participants offer ideas to address specific difficulties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus groups provide individualized attention and idea generation but are not ideal for communicating large amounts of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus groups — disruptive behavior considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: In a small focus group, a difficult participant representing 25–30% of attendees can have a much larger disruptive effect; fewer people are impacted overall, but the disruption is more pronounced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be especially vigilant about participant selection and facilitation in focus groups to mitigate outsized disruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meeting evaluation questionnaire — core items
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard questionnaire items (Likert scale) to evaluate meetings: (1) The meeting achieved its objectives; (2) My personal objectives were achieved; (3) Agenda items were relevant; (4) People stayed focused on agenda items; (5) The meeting was well prepared; (6) Meeting time was used well; (7) The length of the meeting was appropriate. Plus open questions: most useful portions, least useful aspects, actions you will take as a result, other comments/suggestions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use immediate questionnaires for concrete, actionable feedback; combine closed Likert items for comparability and open items for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Michigan Introductory Program — course goals (attitudes, skills, reasoning, knowledge, instruction, persistence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Goals for introductory math courses: establish constructive student attitudes about math (interest, value, likelihood of success, effective learning methods); strengthen general academic skills (critical thinking, writing, clear verbal explanations, collaborative work, responsibility, technology use); improve quantitative reasoning (translate word problems, form reasonable judgments); develop mathematical knowledge (conceptual understanding, basic skills, mathematical sense, problem-solving); improve instruction (instructor commitment, increased student–faculty contact, student-centered approach, instructor satisfaction, ability to organize varied methods); improve student persistence (continued math/science enrollment, more math majors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These program-level goals function as criteria for designing course activities, assessments, and instructor development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching methods encouraged for introductory courses
rubrics_metrics.description: Encouraged methods include interactive lectures with varied questioning techniques, cooperative learning activities, weekly homework assigned to four-person homework teams, expecting and encouraging textbook reading, requiring mathematical writing, integrating hand-held graphing calculators, and emphasizing underlying concepts and real-world problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods support the program goals; instructors are encouraged to use a mix rather than pure lecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical class logistics and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Introductory course sections have up to 32 students, meet three times per week for 90 minutes, with classrooms arranged around four-person tables; instructors should manage group activities and expect regular homework and reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logistics inform feasible activity choices (group work, interactive tasks) and set expectations for pacing and student engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lesson plan structure and in-class activities (sample lesson plan criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sample lesson plans include: clear daily goals (content objectives), assigned reading/homework, opening activities to gather student data and set expectations, interactive lectures, short group/pair activities with specified roles (scribe, graph drawer), timed segments with explicit minute-by-minute plan, return/feedback on quizzes, and reminders about reading/homework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lesson plans prioritize active learning, clear time allocation, student accountability (homework teams), and scaffolding of participation (pair/share before whole-class).
